lines.text: Bronze Age villages, golden temples and kings who kept their land free while empires closed in. This is the story of Thailand.
In the north east, the villagers of Ban Chiang worked bronze and made pots painted with red swirls, more than three thousand years ago.
Much later, in the thirteenth century, a Thai kingdom arose that would grow, slowly, into the country we know as Thailand.
Its first home was Sukhothai, often counted as the first Thai state, where kings favoured Theravada Buddhism.
There King Ram Khamhaeng is credited with creating the Thai alphabet, still used today.
In 1350 Ayutthaya was founded on an island in the river. For four centuries it traded with China, Japan, Persia and Europe.
On the banks of the Chao Phraya, a temple stood that would become Wat Arun, the Temple of Dawn, glittering with Chinese porcelain.
In 1767 Burmese armies destroyed Ayutthaya. Fifteen years later Rama the First founded the Chakri dynasty, which reigns to this day.
He made Bangkok his new capital, on the east bank of the Chao Phraya River, and it grew into a great city.
And there he built the Grand Palace, home of the Emerald Buddha.
King Mongkut, a scholar who had spent years as a monk, opened Siam to the West, and was later made famous by The King and I.
His son Chulalongkorn modernised the kingdom and ended slavery. While its neighbours became colonies, Siam stayed free.
In 1927 Bhumibol Adulyadej was born. He would reign for seventy years, a deeply revered king.
In 1932 a bloodless coup ended absolute monarchy, and Siam became a constitutional kingdom, renamed Thailand a few years later.
In the forties, the government promoted pad thai, stir-fried noodles, as a national dish. It is now Thailand's best-known food.
Thaksin Shinawatra was born, a future prime minister whose supporters and enemies would divide Thai politics for decades.
Vajiralongkorn was born, the son of Bhumibol, who would take the throne in 2016.
In October 1976, student protesters were killed at Thammasat University in Bangkok, a dark day that is still remembered.
In 1997 the Thai currency collapsed, setting off a financial crisis that swept across East Asia.
On Boxing Day 2004, an earthquake off Sumatra sent giant waves across the Indian Ocean, striking Thailand's coast.
In 2014 the army seized power once again, the latest of many coups.
And in 2018 the world watched as twelve boys and their football coach were rescued from a flooded cave after more than two weeks.
Never colonised, often changing, Thailand carries its long story of kings and people into the future.
